content.summary_of_the_paper: The perper addresses a problem of active scene exploration, where a learning method is used to predict how to place the sensor in order to reconstruct the scene in the best way. The next best view is predicted using a new approach to estimate scene model uncertainty leveraging differentiable volumetric rendering. The method is evaluated on a synthetic ABC dataset and a real dataset CO3D.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

The paper proposes to predict the next view uncertainty in the context of a volumetric rendering model, which is new and interesting.

The paper performs exhaustive evaluation using 2 datasets, including one big real dataset (CO3D)

Weaknesses
The paper does not compare to baselines that seem to be straightforward and rather strong. First of all, most of the next best view prediction methods assume depth maps available. The submitted paper assumes only RGB available. However, a combination of RGB and single view depth estimation provides RGBD input, that can be used with the recent baselines. For example, see the baselines here https://openreview.net/pdf?id=foNVYPnQbhk (NeurIPS 2022).

Next, the paper considers Pix2Vox as a single baseline. However, there is a recent Pix2Vox++ publication, that considers alongside with its own method a set of competitive baselines. I would advise to use these baselines as well in the current submission.

The paper does not cover well very important steps. For example, the policies assume a 'random' choice of views best on some 'distance'. Neither 'distance' nor 'random' choice is exactly defined. What is the distance function between the views, and what distribution is chosen to sample the views, how are the parameters of the distribution set?

There is a technical problem: T(t_n) = exp(0) = 1 according to the given formulas....
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: There are some points missing in the paper, see above
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is based on interesting ideas, however the set of baselines in the experiments seems to be very incomplete, and the details in the method seem to be missing
content.correctness: 1: The main claims of the paper are incorrect or not at all supported by theory or empirical results.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.confidence: 2: You are willing to defend your assessment, but it is quite likely that you did not understand the central parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces an occupancy-based reconstruction method. This work explores the occupancy uncertainty accumulated across different views to select the next view for reconstruction. This paper is built on the formulation of NeRF and employs depth and silhouette uncertainty to select the next views.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ The results of the proposed method seem better than the other baselines. 
+ The idea of this work is interesting

- The motivation for selecting views in rendering is not clearly explained. For instance, why do we need to actively select different views? Increasing computational cost or why selecting the next view for rendering is so important? Without clearly exposing the problems to readers, this paper would not be easily understood.

- In the methodology, the authors sequentially select next views for computing occupancy if my understanding is right. Why this is very important? Whether more overlap will improve accuracy or less overlap will encourage coverage of scenes? 

- Assume this method works in practice, how would the authors train the network and collect data on the fly? I think this would be extremely challenging and slowing down the whole reconstruction process.

- In the experiment, this is no comparison with the state-of-the-art methods. Why not provide some results of NeRF or its variants?

- if the object is a ball perfect ball and has distinct texture, whether the uncertainty still works?

- The paper should be better orgnized and some figures are not clear to me. For instance, Fig. 11 is hard for me to understand. The input and the prediction are the same. I am very confused by such figures. I think the final results should be reconstruction, but the results look confusing to me.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: When I read this paper, I found it a bit hard to understand and the figures are not very illustrative. Moreover, the motivation is not clear and the comparison with SOTA is missing.
content.summary_of_the_review: Due to the missing experiments and unclear motivation explanation, I provided my recommendation.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the problem of uncertainty-driven view selection for better implicit 3D reconstruction. In particular, the view selection is based on evaluating the view uncertainty which is calculated based on the silhouette and depth uncertainties. The proposed data-driven view uncertainty leads to better view selection as demonstrated by the evaluation of the performance on two datasets showing the performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
+ View selection can help the model achieves the best performance under a constrained computational budget.
+ Relating the uncertainty with the depth rendering is novel


Weakness:
+ Clarify Eq. (5). The goal is to maximize the view uncertainty and also maximize the distance between the next view and any of the selected views. However, the designed second term in Eq. (5) is meant to minimize the above distance unless the parameter {\lambda_D} is negative. 
+ Is the silhouette uncertainty really necessary? It would be great to have the ablation study about whether of the silhouette uncertainty or the depth uncertainty can be solely treated as the view uncertainty. Will the depth uncertainty be sufficient for defining the view uncertainty?
+ Eq. 3 defines the depth uncertainty not the volume rendering
+ The pipeline. It is not clear to the reviewer about whether it is an online learning process or an iterative stage-wise training method. Does the proposed method rely on a pre-trained model using randomly picked limited number of view images and then include the selected novel view based on the view selection process? 
+ Performance on large scale scene dataset. The experiments on two datasets have shown improved performance based on the proposed next view selection strategy. The two datasets (ABC dataset and  CO3D dataset) for evaluation only includes multiple images of a single object.  It is not clear what the performance of the method would be if it is applied to more complex real scene such as ScanNet. Will it achieve similar performance using a smaller number of images for the reconstruction than the existing implicit method-based 3D reconstruction?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
+ It would be great that the complete training process could be clarified in the paper.
+ The definition of view uncertainty is novel. It would be great to demonstrate that both the silhouette and depth uncertainties are effective in selecting the next best view.
+ Please clarify Eq. 5.
+ Please comment on the possibility of testing the proposed approach on real scene dataset with multiple objects and complex scene layout including severe occlusions.
+ The idea could be reproduced based on the details in the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presented a novel idea of defining the view uncertainty based on the silhouette and the depth uncertainties for implicit scene reconstruction. However, the experiments are only done on data consists of a single object. It is not clear how the proposed next view selection approach will be effective or not in the real complex scene. While the idea is interesting, the results are not strong.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the next-best-view problem for implicit scene reconstruction. The selection policy is based on view uncertainty quantification of a candidate viewpoint. The uncertainty consists of silhouette uncertainty and depth uncertainty, both derived from the uncertainty of occupancy prediction. The training is supervisioned by either 3D occupany ground truth or 2D rendering loss. The method is shown effective on the ABC dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
+ The overall framework is rather simple. The uncertainty quantification are mostly based on the predicted occupacy. The view selection policy is also straightforward. 

Weakness:

- While uncertainty quatification is generally desirable, the next-best-view problem for reduce computation seems less motivated when there exists a line of methods on highly efficient real-time NeRF such as Instant NeRF (https://nvlabs.github.io/instant-ngp/). These methods can process images much more than 5 images and hence make accurate view selection much less relevant. 
- The proposed method is effective  mainly in the simple dataset ABC, while the reconstruction quality is much lower in a realistic dataset CO3D. The reviewer can also foresee even poorer performace in scene-level reconstruction. Hence, the real utility of the method in practice remains questionable. 
- In the comparison experiments against Pix2Vox, it seems the images are selected in the same way as the proposed method. In this case, the performance gap is purely due to the reconstruction method, i.e. occupancy network vs. Pix2Voc? But how does this relate to the key contribution of the paper?
- typo: caption of Fig.3,"In the graph on the left"-> "right"
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Overall the paper is clearly written and easy to follow.
The proposed pipeline is simple, but also somewhat heuristic. The pipeline makes sense but its practical value remains questionable as discussed above. 
The problem of next-best-view problem in implicit scene reconstruction is novel.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents a simple pipeline for the next-best-view selection problem in implicit scene reconstruction. The method is effective in simply dataset but its practical value may be limited.
